speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: Related amendments are also made to other Acts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: It was a significant moment in Singapore’s history – the birth of a new national consciousness.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: These three national symbols gave the people of Singapore our first tangible representations of nationhood – that we are one people – united by a single anthem, identifying with the same state crest and joined by one national flag; we are fellow Singaporeans, fellow citizens forging a shared future together.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Our founding fathers understood the role the national symbols played in unifying the fledging nation.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Mr S Rajaratnam, the then Minister for Culture, laid out how the symbols expressed, and I quote, "the sentiments and aspirations, not of any particular group, party or section, but of the people of Singapore as a whole".

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: He emphasised what each national symbol stood for, like our distinctive Singapore values of "equality" and "progress", and how these symbols represented our "identity and personality".

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The national symbols represented Singapore and the stirrings of a young nation-state.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We had gained self-governance and were no longer subject to – in the words of Mr S Rajaratnam – symbols of "dominance".

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Instead, the national symbols set us apart as a people with our own set of values, beliefs and ideals.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Given their gravity and significance, our pioneering leaders ensured that the symbols were accorded the proper respect.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Since 1959, there have been several important developments in our nation’s journey.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: As our nation developed, Singaporeans also grew in our pride and expression of love for our country.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Increasingly, Singaporeans seek to use the flag and its image to show our national pride and solidarity in ways that were not anticipated back in 1959.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: When it was enacted, the SAFNA Act and Rules deliberately restricted the use of the national flag to preclude the possibility of misuse.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: For instance, the use of the flag as a means of adornment, of advertisement or for any commercial purpose was prohibited.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Unrestricted use of the flag was limited to National Day and occasions of national rejoicing.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The SAFNA Rules were amended over time to accommodate wider usage, but many restrictions were maintained.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Today, Singaporeans wish to express our love for Singapore in many creative ways.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: For example, many interest groups like cycling clubs want to have an image of the flag on their cycling jerseys, for instance.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: During the National Day period, it is very common to see the Singapore flag mounted on the side mirrors of motor vehicles.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Temporary Singapore flag tattoos are also popular with the public and among National Day Parade participants.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Technology has also created new uses for the image of the flag.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Many people now have access to devices and apps that allow them to easily manipulate images and transmit them digitally.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Likewise, the wide use of social media has increased the modes of reproduction and communication of different forms of media, like music and audio clips.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Hence, the Government undertook a review to relook at the national symbol rules.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: MCCY started engaging citizens on the legislative framework and guidelines governing the use of our national symbols in September 2020, done over a two-year period.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: This involved the participation of citizens across several public consultation exercises in the last two years, including polls, focus group discussions and feedback sessions.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The Citizens’ Workgroup for National Symbols was convened in 2021 to discuss and recommend ways to improve the regulation and promotion of the symbols.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The public feedback and recommendations called for greater flexibility in the use of the national symbols, as well as greater clarity on appropriate use and higher safeguards against misuse.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: This feedback has guided our plans for the revised legislation.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: It will also provide more comprehensive protection of the national symbols from misuse.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: One, the inclusion of the symbols like the national pledge, flower and the lion head symbol, which were introduced after 1959, as well as the Presidential symbols and public seal.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Two, the provision for a prescribed person to permit or prohibit uses of the symbols under the regulations, and three, an update on the maximum penalties for infringement of the Act.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: They will now be regarded as national symbols under the Bill.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The national pledge, the national flower as well as the lion head symbols are synonymous with Singapore and evoke immediate recognition and pride among Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The public seal represents the Republic, and the public seal is affixed to important documents of the state, so, it is befitting for it to be recognised as a national symbol of Singapore under the Bill.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: This is appropriate as the President is the Head of State and the symbol of national unity.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The existing SAFNA Rules already regulate the use of the state crest, the national flag and the national anthem.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The Bill will enable the President to make regulations to control the use of Presidential symbols.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The Bill will also enable the President to make regulations to regulate the use of the other national symbols under the Act.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We will extend statutory safeguards to the national pledge and the public seal.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We do not intend to make any new regulations for the lion head symbol or national flower, as these are intended as less restricted symbols for people and organisations to use.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Their inclusion in the Bill is meant to confer on them statutory recognition.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The Citizens' Workgroup for National Symbols, for instance, had suggested that such icons could be recognised as a "tribute to their place in Singapore's history".

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We will continue our practice today of allowing any individual, organisation or company to use the lion head symbol for purposes of identifying with the nation, following prevailing guidelines.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Individuals, organisations and companies are also free to use the image of the national flower.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: All of us in the House will remember, in April 2020, two and a half years ago, the Government responded to calls by Singaporeans to fly the flag as a show of unity and support for one another.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The SAFNA Rules were amended to allow the flag to be displayed outside the typical National Day period, which is from July to September.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: To allow for greater flexibility in future, regulations under the Bill can enable a prescribed person, such as the Minister, to permit the use of a national symbol in appropriate situations.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: This could entail, for example, permitting the display of the national flag outside the National Day period, if warranted by circumstances.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We also intend to make regulations to enable a prescribed person to prohibit certain uses of the symbols, subject to appeal.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: This is to prevent disrespectful uses of the symbols.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: With these new regulations, we can respond more nimbly to legitimate requests to use the national symbols under pre-specified conditions, while also protecting the national symbols from indiscriminate or inappropriate use.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: To provide greater flexibility in the use of the national symbols, we will also review the circumstances and manner in which the symbols may be used.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: For instance, we envisage that the new regulations could take a more permissive stance to allow greater artistic and creative use of an image of the Singapore flag; and to permit the use of images of the national flag on attire outside the National Day period without requiring approval, provided that such use is non-commercial and such use is respectful.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Nonetheless, we must balance the introduction of greater flexibility with proper safeguards against the misuse of our national symbols.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: As Mr S Rajaratnam had pointed out, we need to respect the national symbols for the values, sentiments and ideals they represent.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Rules are critical to ensure that the symbols are not wilfully brought into contempt, ridicule or hatred because such disrespect for our symbols will be an affront to the people of Singapore and the values they represent.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: During the public consultation, many Singaporeans underlined the importance of ensuring that the dignity of the national symbols is upheld even as more flexible use is allowed.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Hence, the third major change we will be making in the Bill is to update the penalties for offences relating to the national symbols and Presidential symbols.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: This sum will not be as effective to serve as a deterrent today as the amount was set in 1959 and has not been updated since.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The penalties for individual offences will be calibrated in the new regulations.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: An example is the burning or desecration of the national flag.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Respect for the symbols is part of the civic and public morality of the nation.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Any affront to our national sovereignty and pride as represented by our symbols must be dealt with seriously.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We should not allow the symbols to be wilfully brought into contempt, ridicule or hatred.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Furthermore, their unauthorised use by private individuals or entities can create false or misleading impressions of links to, or endorsement by, the President or the state.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Such uses could lead to public order issues.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: There is, therefore, a need to regulate the use of the symbols to uphold public morality and order.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: This ensures that prosecutions under the Act are brought in the public interest.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Singaporeans feel a strong sense of ownership of our national symbols and agree that these symbols encapsulate the ideals of what it means to be a Singaporean and what it means to be a member of the Singapore community.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We pay special attention to these symbols because they remind us of who we are, our journey as a nation and the values and aspirations we espouse.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: National symbols are an important part of our national identity and a common rallying point for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I welcome this Bill, which recognises and protects these symbols.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This gives Singaporeans more freedom to express their identity and love for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, there are still some situations where the Government's pre-approval is needed.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This includes the commercial use of our symbols outside of the National Day period or for using the National Anthem.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Independent creatives, in particular, may not have the administrative knowhow to navigate the process.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We should ensure that the bureaucracy of it all does not deter them from innovative, respectful uses of our national symbols.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second clarification relates to the prohibitions under the regulations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our national symbols are not only a source of identity.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They also carry the Singapore brand, signifying the trust and reliability we are known for.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Almost every day, we are seeing new attempts to scam Singaporeans or spread false information, with a large variety of creative tactics.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Earlier this year, investment scammers tried to pass off as GIC and used its logo to try and trick Singaporeans into transferring money to them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I can easily imagine that other scammers might try to use our national symbols, to fake official Government communications, or give a sense of reliability and trick victims into letting their guard down.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Enhanced penalties will deter such fraudulent behaviour and help protect Singaporeans from harm.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My last clarification relates to the President's powers to amend the symbols.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Section 13 allows the aspect or description of any symbol to be amended by notification in the gazette.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Amendment by notification in the Gazette which does not require approval of Parliament appears to be incongruent with the sacrosanct nature of the symbols.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will public consultation be sought before any amendments?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I shall focus my speech on the posture which I hope all stakeholders will take towards this law, not only in Government, but also those in political parties, civil society groups and citizens at large.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And that posture should be to use this law as a reference point for the work of galvanising awareness and respect for our nationhood amongst all citizens.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: All of us can and should be ambassadors and role models for this work, in ways both large and small.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: When people speak of something as symbolic, it sometimes means that it is less valuable and less important.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Less important, perhaps, than material things – money, resources, healthcare, the proverbial bread-and-butter issues.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The bread-and-butter issues that, in some narratives, Singaporean public life is fixated on.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I will say that again – symbols matter!

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The symbols of our nationhood should be viewed by all Singaporeans as precious.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Because they symbolise our hard-fought Independence and our national sovereignty.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It is important because it is equivalent to our national freedom – our freedom to choose our destiny, as a people, through the institutions of our democratic society, the democratic society that our pledge enjoins us to build.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Today, I would like to talk about how we should be one people, regardless of political views and aﬃliation as well.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Some may ﬁnd this an uncomfortable subject to talk about in the context of a conversation about national symbols.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But I think this is an important point to make and expand upon.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It is a view that has some currency, though much less today than it did in the past, from what I can tell.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In truth, I encounter this view less and less.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And I can quite conﬁdently say, from many conversations with Singaporeans, that displaying the ﬂag is not associated with any particular political leaning.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: My Workers' Party colleagues and I are incredibly proud to give out ﬂags on National Day, as are Members of this House from all parties.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And I have met many wonderful Singaporeans, who are true patriots, who belong to multiple political parties.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I have also encountered the view in some quarters that, if one is a Singaporean who disagrees intensely with some aspects of Government policy or the design of political institutions, one, therefore, will ﬁnd the symbols and institutions of this nation alien and unrepresentative.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The people who harbour such sentiments, I would argue, should not be condemned in a very judgemental way.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But it is the task of all of us who care about our country and value our democracy to win over such people, to persuade such people to identify with our national symbols.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In fact, many of the people who are disinterested in the symbols of the nation for such reasons do so precisely because they care passionately about certain principles, ideals and values.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And that is what we need – citizens who care about the greater good and want to play their part in deﬁning it, rather than citizens who do not care about politics or the wider society.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We should, Mdm Deputy Speaker, recognise that the greater danger for our country may not lie in people who are passionate about particular political ideals, but rather people who do not care about politics or anything else going on in the wider society, only bothering to form an opinion when something affects them personally and materially.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: My reply to them has always been, "Please, let us stay and ﬁght to change things in our country".

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: A people who care about politics only in the personal and pecuniary sense, a people who are not invested in the greater good, in what society is and should be, will be a people who are doomed to disappear in the long arc of history.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: So, we should recognise that people who are suspicious of our national symbols may have the best of motives.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: They may be passionate idealists and that should not be dismissed.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It is possible for reasonable citizens to disagree about the design of our national institutions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, some facets of our electoral system or the design of national practices.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, some citizens may disagree that the public expense incurred for the National Day Parade is fully justiﬁed.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I would argue that there can be reasonable points of view on all sides of these questions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And that is exactly how we should resolve such questions – reasonably, respectfully, democratically.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But when it comes to our national symbols, such as our ﬂag, our pledge, our anthem and so on, it is my hope, and I am sure it is the hope of all Members here, that all of us who believe in this democratic society would serve as advocates and role models for the view that our national symbols should be respected by all citizens, across the political spectrum and across the spectrum of views on other matters as well.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Government policies, political ideas, political practices, institutional design – all of these things are subject to the immutable law of change.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: All these things will evolve with time and will be decided democratically now and, one hopes, by future generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The ideas that future generations debate, the technologies and economic arrangements, the big public questions, all of these will evolve and change, probably in ways that we cannot completely foresee now.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But it must be our collective hope that the symbols of our nation endure, along with our nation's sovereignty.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And we should seek this respect for our national symbols, not primarily through heavy-handed legal means, though that has its place.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Rather, we should seek this respect for our national symbols primarily by inspiring citizens with what Singapore is and what it can be, not primarily through law enforcement – though the latter, inevitably, has its place as well; I do not disagree with that.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: How do we ourselves ensure that we remain inspired by this Singapore story and this Singapore cause, so as to be able to inspire others?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Not mainly through prioritising outward, ostentatious displays of national symbols devoid of the real feeling, the heart, the passion.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It is possible to fall into the trap of ritualistic homage to the symbols, while the real passion for what those things symbolise atrophies and dies away.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: So, we should not fall into the trap of saying, for example, that certain HDB blocks are more patriotic because they display more ﬂags and others less so because they display fewer.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: That may not be the case and there could be various reasons why some blocks have more ﬂags than others.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For it is said – that patriotism is the love of one's people, nationalism is the hatred of others.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I hope that ours can be a patriotism that does not seek to validate itself through juxtaposition against some "other" nation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Hatred is a form of energy that can bind a nation, but to the wrong end.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Rather, we should show the world that Singaporeans want to better ourselves and the world without putting anyone else down.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: So, how do we inspire our fellow Singaporeans to respect and love our national symbols?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I think we inspire our citizens and ourselves to respect these precious national symbols by showing the world, through our deeds and words, that these symbols represent, not a perfect country in its ﬁnished form, not a creed set in stone, as many ideas that govern public life will evolve over time.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Rather, these symbols represent something far more precious.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Hope that this place, this land, this people will always strive to get better and better and better in achieving the high ideals of our pledge, one of the symbols being protected by this Bill, even if those ideals never become perfectly embodied in our national life.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Like how, in mathematics, the line of an asymptote inﬁnitely approaches the axis, but never quite touches it.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Hope that we, as a people, will always be free to choose our destiny.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Many Singaporeans would argue, and I include myself here, that aspects of our democratic system are in need of reform.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But that is why we stay and ﬁght to make things better.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Our pledge does not say we already are a democratic society.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Our pledge calls on us to build a democratic society.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It is a work in progress, this building and defending of what has been built.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It is a work that will never end.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And it needs all of us to be builders.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: So, while we may disagree and debate robustly over what the ideals of our pledge concretely mean in day-to-day policies and practice, while we may disagree about many things unconnected to the ideals of the pledge, we should strive to nurture this hope in our own hearts and the hearts of our fellow Singaporeans, all of us – as teachers, colleagues, members of political parties, co-religionists, social media practitioners, opinion leaders, artists, scholars and as parents, as children, as members of families.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This striving should infuse our writing, our social media posts, our scholarship, our words and deeds.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For at the end of the day, while our nation will never be perfect, these symbols represent our hope that the Singaporean people, in this land, will always strive to honour the angels of our better nature.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: When we say something is symbolic, sometimes, it means that it is less valuable or less important, compared to everyday bread-and-butter issues.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The symbols of our nationhood should be viewed by all Singaporeans as precious.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: My Workers' Party colleagues and I are incredibly proud to give out flags on National Day, just like other Members of this House from all parties.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It is not through outward displays of national symbols devoid of real feelings, heart and passion.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It is also not through associating and cultivating hate towards other countries.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: To me, we inspire our citizens and ourselves to respect these precious national symbols by showing the world that these symbols represent hope.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I hope we, as a people, will always be free to choose the life that we desire.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Our pledge calls on us to build a democratic society.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It is a work in progress and we must continue working on it and defending what has been built.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And it needs all of us to build it together.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Many Singaporeans when travelling abroad would have seen how national flags are quite freely used on apparel and luggage bags.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Hence, some of them would question why other countries can be liberal with the use of national symbols whilst what is permitted in other countries may not be allowed in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As such, I welcome the overarching objectives of clause 14 of the Bill, which allows the President to create such regulations relating to our national symbols as the President deems fit.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, I have some clarifications on the Bill and the proposed regulations.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I believe this will be met with the flexibility of making the regulations pursuant to the Bill.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Often, the symbol was used for innocuous purposes, such as to highlight that the product was made in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, such usage may have created the misimpression that the products and services had some form of official endorsement.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Without clear guidelines, businesses may misuse our national symbols to give the impression that the product or service is authorised by the Government.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For example, if security guards who do not work for Government services or public agencies have been spotted with the flag emblem on their uniforms, would that or should that be an offence?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is to ensure that the rules can be properly endorsed but without the need to constantly consult the relevant bodies or burden them with onerous approval processes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Also, as equally important, how will penalties be enforced?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The interpretation of designs can be highly contentious.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Something that is considered disrespectful to someone may be interpreted in an entirely different manner by another.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will there be a framework to provide guidance to our designers?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Does the Government intend to get experts to provide views on its assessment?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If a notice is served on an offender, what is the timeline given to remove the offending act before enforcement action is taken?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Related to this, should there be a need to define "use" and what offences can carry a prosecution?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Is the Bill also intended to cover the use of the national symbols in documents, for example?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Thirdly, Mdm Deputy Speaker, I wish to share some concerns specifically with regard to our national flag.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A question I would like to raise is whether social groups are allowed to use the national flag and other national emblems in their activities.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While this could ostensibly be perceived as a patriotic gesture, it could, in fact, be an attempt to gain wider public support for their activity and their causes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These groups may be locally registered as a society or as a Singapore chapter of a global organisation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They could also be simply a group with a common cause.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Next, there are buildings where you have several flag poles lined up in a row.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I raise this because it could mislead the public by giving the impression that the Government stands alongside a social group and its beliefs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We have read of instances where people have burnt decorations put up for National Day and arrests have been made by the Police.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Last year, a 24-year-old man was charged with cutting and damaging multiple National Day Parade banners and, most recently, a 39-year-old man set a flag on fire, and he was arrested.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A person can also use this as an anti-Government gesture under the pretext of practising his or her religious belief.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Lastly, Mdm Deputy Speaker, Singapore is a young nation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As we journey along, there may be new symbols being introduced.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Does the new legislation cover the addition of new symbols?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Our national flag, especially, represents the values and ideals that we hold dear.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When we were children, we were taught to stand and put our hands over our hearts, facing our national flag and say the national pledge in school.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Our children, including my children, continue this practice today.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Respect for our national symbols is consistent across economic, racial and religious grounds.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Our national symbols are emblems of our unity, thoughts and purpose as a nation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These symbols are not mere pieces of decoration nor objects to be honoured for themselves.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The use of our national flag and symbols thus offers opportunities for Singaporeans to express our patriotism and such patriotism is more important now than ever before.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: After 57 years, we are at a crossroads in our nation's journey.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Our social compact must evolve and respond to both opportunities and challenges.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Through the Forward Singapore exercise, we must come together, examine our values and aspirations, build consensus and, in doing so, refresh our social compact.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Our national symbols play an important and unifying role.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: The significance of our national symbols cannot be understated.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Our national athletes compete, often overseas, in packed stadia.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: When they compete, they do not just represent themselves but the very best of Singapore and what Singapore stands for.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I can tell you, when you are behind the blocks, looking up at stands filled with tens of thousands of spectators and you see a Singapore flag, it fills your heart, and you dig deep to give off more for our country.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: When our athletes win, we often see them take their national flags to the podium to show their patriotism and to acknowledge the support from home which enabled them to achieve greatness and do Singapore proud.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: In 2000, I represented Singapore at the FINA World Cup in Australia.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I swam well enough to make the finals, just two lanes away from the world record holder.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: When I watched the replay on TV that night, I was disappointed to see that next to my name where the Singapore flag should have been was a grey box.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: For reasons I do not know, the TV production crew did not have the graphic of the Singapore flag.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Sad because I felt, in a way, deprived of the ability to share my glory with Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: So, to me, this underscores the significance of our national flag and our national symbols.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: As a former national athlete, I would like to say that every call to the national team is a moment of immense pride.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: It is a privilege which our national athletes do not take lightly.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: It is an honour to wear our national flag emblazoned on the jersey, track suit or swimming cap.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: On the matter of wearing the national flag on the team kits, I would like to ask two questions.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: One, what is the process for National Sports Associations (NSAs) and other organisations to seek approval for the national flag or symbols to be on the team uniform?

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Two, are there guidelines for the type of national teams that can have the national flag or symbols on the uniform?

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: For example, can a youth team wear the national flag on the kit?

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: To conclude, our national symbols evoke immense pride.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: They facilitate opportunities to build solidarity during both challenging times like COVID-19 and during celebratory occasions like international competitions.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: They stir up the national spirit and stimulate civic duty in the elements and colours that remind us of the values Singaporeans should embody.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Most importantly, too, Mdm Deputy Speaker, these symbols are an immediate point of connection, camaraderie and respect amongst our people across the world.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: These are positive things that we, as Parliamentarians, should encourage and I am firm in my support of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Having these displays during significant occasions, such as the Olympics, would be a wonderful way for Singaporeans to express their national pride and unity.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In my constituency, there is a group of citizens who face some challenges if they wish to express their patriotism.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They live in public rental flats where their units face each other.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They have neither available space near their front doors nor at the back, outside the kitchen windows, because that is where they hang their laundry.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope we can facilitate the good intent of these Singaporeans and help them to showcase their national pride.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While the Residents' Committees do hang the flags on parapets or railings of stairwells at these blocks, these are projects by group committees.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For individuals who want to do so on their own initiative, they need some help and support.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would the Ministry share what alternatives there are for these residents?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Bill states that offenders may be fined up to $30,000 or jailed for up to six months, or both, for an offence under the regulations.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Offenders must be given the chance to explain why they made their mistakes.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It should be explained and communicated very clearly to all what constitutes the misuse of national symbols.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What measures has the Ministry planned for to educate members of the public?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The enforcers should also be understanding and not penalise offenders straightaway.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While there will be a minority who intentionally misuse national symbols, more likely than not, these are genuine mistakes.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope they would be advised accordingly instead of being fined.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin):   In my constituency, there are residents who live in public rental flats where their units face each other.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They have no available space to hang the national flag either near their front door or outside the kitchen windows because that is where they hang their laundry.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would the Ministry share what alternatives they have to showcase their patriotism?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Bill states that offenders may be penalised for misuse of national symbols.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: MHA should give the offenders a chance to explain because it could be a misunderstanding.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope the authorities will educate the public on what constitutes misuse of national symbols.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, the five stars on our national flag represent the ideals of Singapore and our national anthem captures the enduring hope and spirit of Singaporeans for progress.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Since the Singapore Arms and Flags and National Anthem Act (SAFNA) was adopted, other symbols, such as the lion head symbol and Vanda Miss Joaquim, which are closely associated with the Singapore identity have also been listed as national symbols.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Although these symbols have come to represent us, they are not accorded the same level of protection from misuse as our state crest, national flag and national anthem because these additional symbols are not covered under SAFNA.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The introduction of the National Symbols Bill to replace SAFNA is thus timely and appropriate and will also help to provide greater flexibility and clarity to the use of national symbols.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Notwithstanding my support for the Bill, I wish to seek clarifications concerning how the national symbols will be regarded and managed after the Bill has been introduced.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some symbols like the Presidential standard, Presidential coat of arms, Presidential seal and public seal would largely not be very commonly used and displayed by the public, unlike other symbols like the national flag, national anthem, national pledge or even the lion head symbol or national flower.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These latter five symbols are those that the public would be most familiar with and are also likely to be the ones that are most used in our everyday life, especially during national occasions.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that the Government will consider allowing members of the public more flexibility in using them so that these symbols can be part of our everyday lives and are close to our hearts instead of being abstract concepts or displays that we occasionally see.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Greater flexibility to access and display these symbols will foster familiarity but still keeping the sense of respect while having the sense of national pride and collective ownership of these symbols that are, essentially, part of our Singapore identity.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Or, from a different perspective, to abolish having a fixed period when the flag can be flown.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If the aim of extending the period from July to September in the past was to allow for a greater display of patriotism, then why not allow Singaporeans and residents to display their love and patriotism for the country all-year round?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The guidelines of use must be explicitly communicated to prevent members of the public and merchants from contravening the use of those symbols.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This was mentioned earlier, I believe, by my Parliamentary colleague, Mr Yip Hon Weng and, at present, I do believe that several companies and merchants have used the lion head symbol on their product packaging to publicise that their products are made in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If yes, would there be an application process to use national symbols on product packaging and publicity collaterals, such as company brochures and banners?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would there be an office set up to process such applications and assess the merits of using national symbols on commercial platforms?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Of course, it would be impossible to capture everything under the law or to have prescriptive guidance for all possible use of the symbols.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many of us would agree that exercising common sense and good judgement in how we should treat our national symbols would suffice on most occasions when the symbols are used.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, there could be some instances where it might not be clear as to just what constitutes "disrespecting a national symbol".

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, if you search for "Singapore national anthem on electric guitar" on the Internet, which some of us might be tempted to do that right now on our devices, you will find a mellow, reggae-inspired version of "Majulah Singapura" on YouTube.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Personally, I did not find that remix or that version of our national anthem offensive or disrespectful.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In fact, the comments on the remix were all largely positive.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, would such a remix or interpretation of our national anthem be considered disrespectful under the new law and lead to a financial penalty or some measures taken against the artiste?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Similarly, if parts of, or even the entire Singapore pledge were fused into a performance piece, would that be okay, or would the performer be taken to task if he or she did not get prior clearance from the authorities?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There was also the case of a migrant worker who loved Singapore so much that he got the lion head symbol tattooed on the back of his neck.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would this be allowed under the new proposed laws?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singaporeans should thus be more acquainted with the history of the symbols and what those symbols stand for.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Safeguards, of course, notwithstanding, I end my speech in firm support of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The national symbols belong to Singapore and all Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: They embody our most cherished ideals, values and aspirations.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: They are a manifestation of our shared identity.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: As our founding Prime Minister, the late Mr Lee Kuan Yew believed, the symbols have and I quote, "every reason to endure as the emblems of the state" and "will evoke loyalty and unity in our people".

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The Bill reflects our intention to uphold and cultivate this unity and patriotic sense of collective ownership of the national symbols, like what Mr Leon Perera mentioned earlier.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We have consulted citizens and fellow Singaporeans widely over the last two years for this Bill, which reflects the wishes and suggestions of what we have heard and learned from Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Singaporeans are proud of the national symbols and recognise the duty of respect we have towards them.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: As we seek to replace the SAFNA Act with the National Symbols Act, Members Mr Louis Ng and Mr Yip Hon Weng have asked for greater clarity on possible changes to the symbols.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Mr Louis Ng observed that the Bill allows the aspect or description of any symbol to be, and I quote, "amended by notification in the gazette without requiring the approval of Parliament" and "appears to be incongruent with the sacrosanct nature of the symbols." He wishes to know the circumstances in which such amendments may be made and if the public would be consulted before any such amendments.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: As Mr Louis Ng pointed out, the national symbols and their official meanings are well-established and widely recognised by Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We do not envisage this clause to be used frequently or in any significant way.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Under the SAFNA Act, the description of the national anthem, state crest and national flag are all already set out in the subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: In exercising the power of amendment under clause 13, the President will be acting on the advice of the Cabinet.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: For now, we do not foresee the need or wish to add any new national symbols.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The Citizens' Workgroup for National Symbols had studied this matter and had polled Singaporeans for their views in March 2021.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Most respondents had "reflected a preference for no new additions to the current set of national symbols".

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I want to assure Members that any significant changes to the symbols will not be undertaken lightly.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: There will be ways, apart from the law, that we can recognise and appreciate significant symbols and images that may evolve in the future as we continue to build our sense of national identity.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I want to thank all the six Members who spoke passionately, who spoke with a lot of conviction for their support to do more to let Singaporeans express their national pride through our national symbols, such as Mr Leon Perera and also Mr Darryl David.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Mr Darryl David asked if we could consider extending or even abolishing the fixed period when the flag could be flown.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: However, those we engaged also consistently raised the concern that over-liberalisation would diminish the stature of the symbols and lead to more incidences of misuse.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Mr Louis Ng, Mr Mark Chay, Mr Darryl David and Mr Yip Hong Weng asked about the guidelines on the use of the national symbols and the process by which permission for their use can be sought.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Mr Louis Ng highlighted the need for the approval process to be "accessible, low-cost, and simple" enough for well-intentioned individuals, such as independent creatives.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: On a related note, Mr Mark Chay asked about the approval process for NSAs to use the national flag or other symbols on their sporting attire and whether there are guidelines under which national teams can use the flag or other symbols on their uniforms.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Mr Darryl David, in his speech, also asked about the approval process for using the lion head symbol on product packaging and suggested that the guidelines be explicitly communicated to prevent the public and merchants from contravening the use of those symbols.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Similarly, during his speech, Mr Yip Hon Weng asked for more clarity on the usage and design guidelines for the national symbols, including (a) their uses in commercial advertisements; (b) how detailed the proposed regulations will be; (c) clearer examples on how the image of the national flag could be used on attire, decoration and products in cases where no official approval is required; and (d) if a guiding framework will be developed to help designers navigate this process.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We wish for fellow Singaporeans to have more opportunities to display and celebrate their national pride.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: As we allow for more flexibility in the use of the symbols, we will also ensure that the guidelines on their usage are easily accessible and easily understood, especially for cases where no prior approvals will be needed.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Presently, we have in place a simple process for anyone wishing to seek approval for the use of a national symbol.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Depending on the context of the nature of use, this process will continue after the Bill comes into effect.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: This process will also remain free for users.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: As pointed out by Mr Mark Chay, there are specific administrative processes required to use the national symbols in some cases, like in the instance of the attire for Team Singapore athletes.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: This is to ensure the accurate and dignified representation of our country outside Singapore by our sporting ambassadors.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: For example, currently, approvals for use of the image of the flag on the team attire for national athletes are channelled through Sport Singapore, the public body providing recognition and support for NSAs.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Approvals for other organisations that wish to use the national flag on their attire, including youth teams that may not belong to any NSA, is granted through MCCY on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: However, Sport Singapore will continue to work closely with NSAs to advise them on the respectful use of the image of the flag on their team attire.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: All updates and changes regarding the use of the symbols will be clearly shown on the National Heritage Board (NHB)'s website when the subsidiary legislation has been enacted.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We agree with both Mr Yip Hon Weng and Mr Darryl David that clear and accessible guidelines on the use of the national symbols are important to give the public and users the assurance that the national symbols are treated with due respect.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Currently, those who wish to use the national symbols can find on the NHB website the background, guidelines, FAQs and requirements for use of each symbol.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Individuals or organisations can seek clarification or report prima facie misuse of a national symbol by submitting a simple enquiry form via the NHB website.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The question of how we ought to define disrespectful use is an important one which had come up in our public engagements, including those with the creative industry.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Some clear examples of disrespectful use which we have encountered and dealt with in the past include works with the image of the flag alongside images featuring nudity and violence.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Using the design of the flag on undergarments is considered disrespectful use.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Displaying images of a damaged or a torn flag in the context of denigrating the nation is considered disrespectful use.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng's example of applying an image of the flag on paraphernalia to be burned as religious offerings would fall into this category.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Very often, and in many cases, the context, nature of use and intent behind the use of the symbols have to be carefully considered to determine if the usage of the image was disrespectful or inappropriate – the context, nature of use, intent of the use.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Mr Darryl David brought up several examples, such as remixing the national anthem, using the pledge in a performance, or getting a tattoo, a permanent tattoo, not a temporary one as I had mentioned in my opening speech, getting a tattoo image of the lion head.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: To reduce ambiguity, I want to assure Members we intend to develop more specific guidelines based on clearly articulated principles to establish common standards of what might constitute respectful and what might constitute disrespectful treatment of the national symbols.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: For instance, whether on attire or decoration, any use of the image of the flag should avoid it being easily soiled or stepped upon.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: For other symbols like the national anthem, guidelines would include using the complete official lyrics and music when rearranging the anthem and ensuring that the anthem is not incorporated into any other medley or composition.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: So, if you think about it, the use of the stop order would reduce uncertainty about what constitutes an offence.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: This will also help to clearly address cases of misuse.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Like what Mr Darryl David mentioned in his speech, it is really not possible for the guidelines to cover all possible scenarios.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We are also very mindful that the guidelines should not be too rigid or too prescriptive, as this might inhibit creativity and greater use of the national symbols.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I want to assure all Members in the House that MCCY will carefully consider the points which have been raised by Members in our next steps of development.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I want to assure everyone that we aim to provide as much clarity on the usage and design guidelines for the national symbols as we can.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We will also continue to keep open channels for the public to feed back or seek clarification on their intended use of the national symbols or to report any potential misuse.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I also want to assure the Members that we aim to strike a good balance between giving Singaporeans the latitude to use the national symbols creatively and ensuring due respect for them.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Mr Louis Ng, Ms Joan Pereira, Mr Leon Perera and Mr Yip Hon Weng raised questions about penalties for those who knowingly, or unknowingly, misuse the national symbols under the Bill.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Before I address them in detail, I would like to reiterate the principles underpinning the proposed legislative framework.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The objective here is to provide greater flexibility for members of the public to use the national symbols to identify with our nation.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I think Members would agree with me that with greater flexibility comes greater responsibility.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: This really means that stronger safeguards are necessary to ensure that individuals and organisations use the national symbols in a respectful manner.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Penalties should be reasonable and commensurate with the severity of the misuse.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We envision that the broad categories of offences under the new regulations will include, for example, using a national or Presidential symbol that conveys state sanction or authority without permission; using a national or Presidential symbol outside the prescribed manner; and failure to cease disrespectful use when ordered to do so.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: So, the questions raised by Mr Louis Ng, Ms Joan Pereira and Mr Yip Hon Weng pertain to each of the three categories I have just mentioned.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: On the other hand, as Mr Leon Perera mentioned, minor infractions, such as the inadvertent failure to remove the flag after a designated display period, will not incur such penalties.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked if an image of the flag on the uniforms of security guards would be viewed as an offence.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I want to assure him and all the Members who spoke that, in practice, MCCY and NHB do not impose penalties as a first course of action.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Our approach for these cases would be to educate and inform the public on the guidelines and request that the flag be removed.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: For other similar cases of misuse, such as inadvertently hanging the flag the wrong way, we also find that this approach of public education and raising public awareness works very well.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We agree with Ms Joan Pereira and Mr Leon Perera about the importance of public education and public awareness to prevent any unintentional misuse of the national symbols.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Individuals who have inadvertently misused a symbol should be given a chance to explain and not be penalised for an honest mistake.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: In addition, we note Ms Joan Pereira's observation about the lack of a suitable area to display the flag for certain residents, such as those in public rental housing flats.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Ms Joan Pereira will be happy to note that MCCY will take this into consideration and address this in our engagements with other public agencies as part of our plans to promote respectful use of the flag.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We share Ms Joan Pereira's view on the broader point of ensuring that everyone has the opportunity to demonstrate their love for the country, through the display of the national flag from their homes and with the rest of the community.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Depending on the facts, misuse of the symbols could also amount to offences under other legislation.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked about the number of cases prosecuted under the current SAFNA Act and Rules.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: For example, in 2018, a social media user posted an image of our national flag being torn apart to reveal an image of another country's flag.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The user was issued a stern warning for contravention of the SAFNA Rules.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: While there has not been any prosecutions and composition of offences under the SAFNA Act and Rules, certain misuses of the national symbols were dealt with under other legislation, such as the Penal Code 1871, where some of the offenders were punished with imprisonment.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Singaporeans have, generally, treated the National Symbols with respect and we are confident that they will continue to do so.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked about the time given to an offender to cease disrespectful use of a symbol before enforcement action is taken after a stop order.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I want to assure him that we will provide a reasonable timeframe that would give the user sufficient time to explain his or her position and use.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Further details, such as the prescribed person and the appeals authority and processes, will be set out in the subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The National Emblems (Control of Display) Act 1949 governs the display of foreign national emblems in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng raised a question about this Act, how it would be amended.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I agree with her that most people do not set out to intentionally misuse the symbols.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: As we give expression to the love we have for Singapore, we affirm our identity as a nation, as one united people, as one Singapore.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The symbols, under the National Symbols Bill will serve as visual reminders of our aspirations and obligations as Singaporeans and inspire us to greater unity and purpose.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: On that note, I thank all the six Members for their support of the Bill.
